text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the equilibrium radius from photon and recombination balance, solve volume growth, and explain the neglect of gas motion. Connect to foundations: Atomic light and starlight: why 10.2 eV? ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Count ionizing photons, not just luminosity Hot stars create regions of ionized hydrogen, called H II regions. Ionizing hydrogen requires a photon of at least 13.6 eV, unlike the 10.2 eV Lyα transition. The relevant input is the rate of photons above this threshold, rather than total stellar luminosity alone. S ≡ ∫ν₀∞Lνhνdν, hν₀ = 13.6 eV S has units s−1: divide spectral luminosity by photon energy before integrating. Assume pure hydrogen of uniform nucleus density nH, a constant source S, no dust, and a nearly fully ionized interior. 02Count the recombinations that remove ions Recombination occurs at rate αnenp. Direct recombination to the ground state emits another ionizing photon. In the on-the-spot approximation, that photon is absorbed nearby, so this event does not require a new stellar photon in the net ionization budget. αB(10⁴ K) ≈ 2.6 × 10−13 cm³ s−1 dNrecdt dV = αBnenp ≈ αBnH² The Case B coefficient αB counts recombinations to excited states and is supplied at the assumed temperature. The same photon budget does not apply unchanged to a cloud that leaks ionizing photons or absorbs many of them in dust. 03Balance supply and consumption to find the radius Let the ionized volume be V = 4πR³/3. In equilibrium, the supplied photon rate equals the integrated net recombination rate. At constant density, solving this volume balance gives the radius directly. S = 4π3RS³αBnH² RS = [3S4παBnH²]1/3 For S = 1049 s−1, nH = 100 cm−3, and the stated coefficient, RS is about 3.15 pc. Doubling density quadruples recombinations per unit volume and reduces the radius by 2−2/3. 04Excess photons ionize newly reached gas Start with neutral gas. During growth, some photons replace recombinations in the existing ionized volume, while the remainder ionizes nHdV/dt newly reached atoms. The gas stays fixed; only the ionization boundary advances. nHdVdt = S−αBnH²V dVdt+Vtrec = SnH, trec = 1αBnH Set V = VS + W. Then W′ = −W/trec, so W decays exponentially. Apply V(0) = 0 and take the cube root only after obtaining the volume. V(t) = VS[1−e−t/trec] R(t) = RS[1−e−t/trec]1/3 05An ionization radius versus an expanding H II region In the example, trec is about 1.22 × 10³ yr. At one recombination time, volume is about 63% and radius about 86% of equilibrium. Radius does not advance linearly with time. The circle marks an ionization boundary, not the velocity of all the gas. Extrapolating this instantaneous, nonrelativistic photon budget to t → 0 formally produces infinite front speed. Do not apply it before light-travel times of order R/c or to relativistic fronts. Later, heated gas can expand under pressure and drive shocks; that phase requires gas dynamics. In a clumpy medium, recombinations depend on the average of nenp, not simply the square of mean density. A measured radius alone does not uniquely determine stellar age or photon output without checking leakage, dust, density structure, and dynamical stage. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Multiply the ionizing-photon rate by eight and hydrogen-nucleus density by two. How do equilibrium radius and recombination time change? Show the answer and reasoning RS ∝ (S/nH²)1/3 increases by 21/3, about 1.26. The recombination time 1/(αB nH) halves. This holds at fixed temperature and αB, for fully ionized pure hydrogen with ne = np = nH. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
